MHI is one of the core companies of the [[Mitsubishi Group]] and its automobile division is the predecessor of [[Mitsubishi Motors]]. MHI's products include [[aerospace]] and [[Automotive industry|automotive]] components, [[Air conditioning|air conditioners]], [[elevator]]s, [[Forklift|forklift trucks]], [[Hydraulic machinery|hydraulic equipment]], [[Printing|printing machines]], [[missile]]s, [[tank]]s,{{Cite web|title=Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Ltd. Global Website {{!}} History : Sagamihara Machinery Works|url=https://www.mhi.com/company/location/sagamiharaw/history|access-date=16 June 2021|website=Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Ltd.|language=en}} [[Electric power system|power systems]], [[ship]]s, [[aircraft]], [[Rail transport|railway systems]], and space [[launch vehicle]]s.{{cite web|url=http://www.mhi.co.jp/en/products/index.html|title=Products|access-date=27 December 2011|publisher=Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Ltd.|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120105004630/http://www.mhi.co.jp/en/products/index.html|archive-date=5 January 2012}}{{Cite web|title=Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Ltd. Global Website {{!}} PRODUCTS|url=https://www.mhi.com/products|access-date=20 July 2020|website=Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Ltd.|language=en}} Through its defense-related activities, it is the world's 32nd-largest [[defense contractor]] measured by 2024 arms revenues and the largest based in Japan.{{Cite web|url=https://www.sipri.org/visualizations/2025/sipri-top-100-arms-producing-and-military-services-companies-world-2024|title=The SIPRI Top 100 arms-producing and military services companies in the world, 2024|publisher=Stockholm International Peace Research Institute |date=December 2025|access-date=7 May 2026}} {{TOC limit|limit=3}} ==History== [[File:Big Cranes Mitsubishi.jpg|thumb|upright|left|The Mitsubishi Dockyard at Nagasaki, Meiji Period]] In 1857, at the request of the [[Tokugawa Shogunate]], a group of [[Dutch people|Dutch]] engineers were invited, including Dutch naval engineer Hendrik Hardes, and began work on the ''Nagasaki Yotetsusho'' ({{lang|ja|長崎鎔鉄所}}), a modern, Western-style [[foundry]] and shipyard near the Dutch settlement of [[Dejima]], at [[Nagasaki, Nagasaki|Nagasaki]].{{cite web|url=http://www.mhi.co.jp/en/nsmw/introduction/history/index.html|publisher=Nagasaki Shipyard & Machinery Works|title=History| url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110807050917/http://www.mhi.co.jp/en/nsmw/introduction/history/index.html|archive-date=7 August 2011}}Fukasaku (1992), p. 17. This was renamed ''Nagasaki Seitetsusho'' ({{lang|ja|長崎製鉄所}}) Nagasaki Iron (Steel) Foundry in 1860, and construction was completed in 1861. Following the [[Meiji Restoration]] of 1868, the shipyard was placed under control of the new [[Government of Meiji Japan]]. The first dry dock was completed in 1879. In 1884, [[Iwasaki Yatarō]], the founder of Mitsubishi, leased the ''Nagasaki [[Ironworks|Seitetsusho]]'' from the Japanese government, renamed it the ''Nagasaki Shipyard & Machinery Works'' ({{lang|ja|長崎造船機械工}}) and entered the shipbuilding business on a large scale. Iwasaki purchased the shipyards outright in 1887. In 1891, "Mitsubishi Heavy Industries - Yokohama Machinery Works" was started as ''Yokohama Dock Company, Ltd''. Its main business was ship repairs, to which it added ship servicing by 1897.{{cite web|url=http://www.mhi.co.jp/en/ydmw/introduction/outline/index.html|publisher=Yokohama Machinery Works|title=Outline| url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110807051657/http://www.mhi.co.jp/en/ydmw/introduction/outline/index.html|archive-date=7 August 2011}} The works was renamed ''Mitsubishi Shipyard of Mitsubishi [[Gōshi gaisha|Goshi Kaisha]]'' in 1893 and additional [[dry dock]]s were completed in 1896 and 1905. The "Mitsubishi Heavy Industries - Shimonoseki Shipyard & Machinery Works" was established in 1914. It produced industrial machinery and merchant ships.{{cite web|url=http://www.mhi.co.jp/en/ssmw/introduction/outline/index.html|publisher=Shimonoseki Shipyard & Machinery Works|title=Outline| url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110807052446/http://www.mhi.co.jp/en/ssmw/introduction/outline/index.html|archive-date=7 August 2011}} [[File:Tosa launch.jpg|thumb|upright|The launch of battleship [[Japanese battleship Tosa|''Tosa'']] at the Nagasaki Shipyard, 1921]] The Nagasaki company was renamed ''Mitsubishi Shipbuilding & Engineering Company, Ltd.'' in 1917 and again renamed as ''Mitsubishi Heavy Industries'' in 1934. It became the largest private firm in Japan, active in the manufacture of ships, heavy machinery, airplanes and railway cars. Mitsubishi Heavy Industries merged with the Yokohama Dock Company in 1935. From its inception, the Mitsubishi Nagasaki shipyards were heavily involved in contracts for the [[Imperial Japanese Navy]]. The largest [[battleship]] [[Japanese battleship Musashi|''Musashi'']] was completed at Nagasaki in 1942. These connections made Nagasaki a target for [[strategic bombing]] during [[World War II]] by the [[Allies of World War II|Allied]] [[air force]]s, which later dropped an [[nuclear weapon|atomic bomb]] on the city on 9 August 1945. This attack, following the [[Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki|atomic bombing]] of [[Hiroshima]] three days earlier, dealt a devastating blow to the Japanese leadership, contributing to the [[surrender of Japan]] six days later. The ''Kobe Shipyard of Mitsubishi Goshi Kaisha'' was established in 1905. The Kobe Shipyard merged with Mitsubishi Heavy Industries in 1934. The Kobe Shipyard constructed the ocean liner ''Argentina Maru'' (later repurposed as the [[aircraft carrier]] ''[[Japanese aircraft carrier Kaiyo|Kaiyo]]''), and the submarines the ''[[Japanese submarine I-19|I-19]]'' and ''[[Japanese submarine I-25|I-25]]''.{{cite web|url=http://www.mhi.co.jp/en/kobe/introduction/history/briefhistory/index.html|publisher=Kobe Shipyard & Machinery Works|title=Brief History| url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110807052529/http://www.mhi.co.jp/en/kobe/introduction/history/briefhistory/index.html|archive-date=7 August 2011}} Following the dissolution of the ''[[zaibatsu]]'' after the surrender of Japan at the end of [[World War II]], Mitsubishi divided into three companies in January 1950: Mitsubishi Nagasaki became ''West Japan Heavy Industries, Ltd'', the Kobe Shipyard became ''Central Japan Heavy-Industries, Ltd.'', and the Yokohama branch became East Japan Heavy-Industries, Ltd. On 28 April 1952 the [[Occupation of Japan]] ended, which meant that the ban on using ''zaibatsu'' names was lifted.{{cite web | url = http://www.mikipress.com/m-base/2019/08/85-1.html | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20191219173944/http://www.mikipress.com/m-base/2019/08/85-1.html | archive-date = 19 December 2019 | title = 「モーターファン」誌1952年1月号に載った広告 | trans-title = Advertising in the January 1952 issue of "Motorfan" magazine | date = 27 August 2019 | work = M-Base | last = Toma | first = Setsuo | number = 85 | publisher = Miki Press | language = ja }} Accordingly, all three companies changed names again on 7 May 1952: West Japan Heavy Industries (the Nagasaki Shipyard) was renamed ''Mitsubishi Shipbuilding & Engineering Co., Ltd.'', Central Japan Heavy Industries, Ltd. was renamed Shin-Mitsubishi Jukogyo K.K. (also [[trade name|trading as]] ''Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Reorganized, Ltd.'';{{cite tweet|number=1347452110044975104|user=nandaumanosuke2|title=一昨日掘ったら出てきたシリーズ（てきとう 新三菱重工業時代の液化塩素用タンク車タサ2300英文カタログ 日本語版もあったはず。 |date=8 January 2021}} ''shin'' meaning "New"), while East Japan Heavy-Industries became Mitsubishi Nippon Heavy Industries. In 1964, the three independent companies from the 1950 break-up were merged into Shin-Mitsubishi Jukogyo and became Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Ltd. The Nagasaki works was renamed the ''Nagasaki Shipyard & Engine Works''. The Kobe works was renamed the 'Mitsubishi Heavy Industries - Kobe Shipyard & Machinery Works'.{{cite web|url=http://www.mhi.co.jp/en/kobe/introduction/outline/index.html|publisher=Kobe Shipyard & Machinery Works|title=Outline| url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110807052202/http://www.mhi.co.jp/en/kobe/introduction/outline/index.html|archive-date=7 August 2011}} In 1970, MHI's automobile parts department became an independent company as [[Mitsubishi Motors]]. In 1974, its Tokyo headquarters was targeted in a [[1974 Mitsubishi Heavy Industries bombing|bombing that killed eight people]]. MHI participated in a ¥540 billion emergency rescue of Mitsubishi Motors in January 2005, in partnership with [[Mitsubishi Corporation]] and [[Mitsubishi Tokyo Financial Group]].{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/01/28/business/worldbusiness/28iht-mitsu.html|title=Mitsubishi's rocky road|access-date=17 July 2012|newspaper=The New York Times| date=29 January 2005}}{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/business/4214655.stm|title=Mitsubishi seeks $5.2bn bail out |access-date=17 July 2012|work=BBC News| date=28 January 2005}} As part of the rescue, MHI acquired ¥50 billion of Mitsubishi Motors stock, increasing its ownership stake to 15 percent and making the automaker an affiliate again. The emergency rescue was carried out 4 years after a product recall scandal in Japan that was triggered by accusations of Mitsubishi Motors allegedly trying to systematically hide manufacturing defects to avoid recalls, and marketing problems in the US. In 1994, MHI opened the [[Mitsubishi Minatomirai Industrial Museum]] in Yokohama which is mainly a museum for kids to experience science and technology.{{Cite web|url=https://www.mhi.com/company/overview/museum/minatomirai/about_museum|title=Mitsubishi Minatomirai Industrial Museum | About|website=Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Ltd.}} In October 2009, MHI news|url=http://uk.reuters.com/article/uk-hitachi-mitsubishi-idUKTRE7730FY20110804|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160306101357/http://uk.reuters.com/article/uk-hitachi-mitsubishi-idUKTRE7730FY20110804|url-status=dead|archive-date=6 Engineering|language=en-US}} In June 2014, [[Siemens]] and MHI announced their formation of joint ventures to bid for [[Alstom]]'s troubled energy and transportation businesses (in locomotives, steam turbines, and aircraft engines). A rival bid by [[General Electric]] (GE) has been criticized by French government sources, who consider Alstom's operations as a "vital national interest" at a moment when the French unemployment level stands above 10% and some voters are turning towards the conservative party.{{Cite web|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-alstom-siemens-offer-idUSKBN0ER0MC20140616|title=Siemens and Mitsubishi challenge GE with Alstom offer|work=U.S. |last1=Jens Hack |first1=Natalie Huet |date=16 June 2014 }} GE's proposal ultimately prevailed.{{Cite web|title=GE Completes Acquisition of Alstom Power and Grid Businesses {{!}} GE News|url=https://www.ge.com/news/press-releases/ge-completes-acquisition-alstom-power-and-grid-businesses|access-date=22 July 2020|website=www.ge.com|language=en}} MHI had entered the high-speed train business in 1995, with the manufacture of the [[SCMaglev and Railway Park#Exhibits|MLX01 SCMaglev car]], a business it exited in 2017 after struggling with the development costs of the [[Mitsubishi SpaceJet]], and disagreements with [[Central Japan Railway Company]] over the manufacturing costs of the SCMaglev cars.{{Cite web|url=https://asia.nikkei.com/Business/Mitsubishi-Heavy-to-back-out-of-maglev-train-project|title = Mitsubishi Heavy to back out of maglev train project}} In February 2021, MHI sold its machine tools business MHI Machine Tool Co. to [[Nidec]].{{Cite news|date=5 February 2021|title=Japan's Nidec to buy MHI's machine tool unit as it bolsters EV motor business|language=en|work=Reuters|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/nidec-mhi-idUSASA01P17|access-date=30 March 2021}} In June 2024, MHI announced it will cease newspaper [[rotary printing press]] production due to declining demand. At the time the company held a 50% share of the Japanese rotary press market.{{Cite web |date=28 June 2024 |title=Mitsubishi Heavy to End Newspaper Rotary Press Production |url=https://www.nippon.com/en/news/yjj2024062801017/ |access-date=29 June 2024 |website=nippon.com |language=en |archive-date=29 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240629041115/https://www.nippon.com/en/news/yjj2024062801017/ |url-status=dead }} ==Operations== [[File:Mitsubishi Heavy Industries Yokohama Building -01.jpg|thumb|upright|Mitsubishi Heavy Industries building in [[Yokohama]], [[Japan]]]] ===Aerospace=== MHI has aerospace facilities in [[Nagoya]], [[Aichi]], [[Komaki, Aichi]] and [[Mississauga, Canada]]. In the 1950s, the company began to re-enter the aerospace industry in earnest. Along with other major Japanese companies it was involved in design and production of the [[NAMC YS-11]], the first Japanese airliner to enter production after World War II.{{cn|date=July 2026}} In 1956, work started on the design of the [[Mitsubishi MU-2]], which became the company's first postwar aircraft design.[http://www.airliners.net/aircraft-data/mitsubishi-mu-2/288 Mitsubishi MU-2] ''airliners.net'' Retrieved 7 December 2016 In the defense sector, MHI has produced jet fighters for the [[Japan Air Self-Defense Force]] and anti-submarine helicopters for the [[Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force]], as well as aero-engines, missiles and torpedoes. It produced [[North American F-86 Sabre]], [[Lockheed F-104 Starfighter]] and [[McDonnell Douglas F-4 Phantom II]] fighters. It manufactured 139 [[Mitsubishi F-15J]] fighter aircraft from 1981 and produced 200 [[Sikorsky S-70]] family [[Mitsubishi H-60]] helicopters from 1989, in both cases under license production. The company also plays an important role in the Japanese Ballistic Missile Defense System program. In the space systems sector, MHI is the producer of the former [[H-IIA]] and [[H-IIB]]; and current [[H3 (rocket)|H3]] launch vehicles, Japan's main rockets, and provides launch services for national institutions and companies around the world. The clients include [[JAXA]], [[Korea Aerospace Research Institute|KARI]], [[Mohammed bin Rashid Space Centre]], and [[Inmarsat]].{{Cite web|title=Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Ltd. Global Website {{!}} MHI Receives Order for Satellite Launch Services from EIAST of UAE|url=https://www.mhi.com/news/story/1503091878.html|access-date=20 July 2020|website=Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Ltd.|date=9 March 2015 |language=en}}{{Cite web|date=19 July 2020|title=UAE's Amal spacecraft rockets toward Mars in Arab world 1st|url=https://www.kaaltv.com/news/united-arab-emirates-spacecraft-blasts-off-from-japan/5799721/|access-date=20 July 2020|website=ABC 6 NEWS|language=en|archive-date=20 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200720032645/https://www.kaaltv.com/news/united-arab-emirates-spacecraft-blasts-off-from-japan/5799721/|url-status=dead}}{{Cite web|title=Inmarsat first customer for new MHI launch vehicle - News|url=https://www.inmarsat.com/news/inmarsat-first-customer-for-new-mhi-launch-vehicle/|access-date=20 July 2020|website=Inmarsat|date=6 December 2018 |language=en-US}} The company is also involved in the [[International Space Station]] program as a [[Cargo spacecraft|cargo spaceship]] contractor.{{Cite web|first=Tariq |last=Malik |title=Japanese HTV cargo ship, the last of its kind, launches to International Space Station|url=https://www.space.com/japanese-htv-cargo-ship-final-launch-success.html|access-date=20 July 2020|website=Space.com|date=20 May 2020|language=en}} On 1 April 2008, MHI established [[Mitsubishi Aircraft Corporation]] as a subsidiary to develop and produce the MRJ or [[Mitsubishi Regional Jet]], a 70 to 90 passenger regional airliner. MHI is the majority shareholder of the new company, with [[Toyota|Toyota Motor Corporation]] owning 10%.{{cite web|url=http://en.ce.cn/World/biz/200805/23/t20080523_15587864.shtml|title=Toyota to sink $67.2 mln in Mitsubishi passenger jet _World Biz--China Economic Net|access-date=7 February 2017|archive-date=18 May 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110518042359/http://en.ce.cn/World/biz/200805/23/t20080523_15587864.shtml|url-status=dead}} On 12 December 2012, MHI acquired [[Pratt & Whitney#Pratt & Whitney Power Systems|Pratt & Whitney Power Systems]], the small gas turbine business of [[United Technologies Corporation|United Technologies]].[https://www.reuters.com/article/unitedtechnolgies-divestiture-idCNL4N09M42420121212 United Tech to sell P&W power systems unit to Mitsubishi Heavy]. ''Reuters''. 12 December 2012. Retrieved 30 April 2021. 2024|publisher=Mitsubishi Heavy Industries}} In June 2014, the company joined four other major Japanese companies in signing an agreement to build parts for [[Boeing 777X|Boeing's 777X aircraft]].{{cite news|title=Boeing enters pact with Japanese consortium for supply of 777X plane parts|url=http://www.chicagochronicle.com/index.php/sid/222852667/scat/3a8a80d6f705f8cc/ht/Boeing-enters-pact-with-Japanese-consortium-for-supply-of-777X-plane-parts|access-date=12 June |work=Flightglobal.com |date=6 June 2019}} The deal includes two service centres in Canada and two in the US, as well as the type certificates for the CRJ.{{cite news |last1=Chua |first1=Alfred Bombardier will retain its assembly facility at [[Montréal-Mirabel International Airport|Mirabel]], near [[Montreal]], Canada, and will continue to produce the CRJ on behalf of MHI until the current order backlog is complete.{{cite news |title=Mitsubishi, Bombardier reach agreement to acquire CRJ program |url=https://leehamnews.com/2019/06/25/mitsubishi-bombardier-reach-agreement-to-acquire-crj-program/ |work=Leeham News and Analysis |date=25 June 2019}} In early May 2020, MHI confirmed that all conditions had been met and that the transaction would be closed on 1 June.{{cite news |last1=Hemmerdinger |first1=Jon |title=Mitsubishi to close CRJ purchase on 1 June |url=https://www.flightglobal.com/airframers/mitsubishi-to-close-crj-purchase-on-1-june/138259.article |work=Flight Global |date=7 May 2020 |language=en}} The acquired aviation unit was then renamed Global Website {{!}} Mitsubishi Heavy Industries Ltd. and Bombardier Inc. have agreed on a 1 June 2020 closing date for the transaction pertaining to the acquisition of Canadair Regional Jet Program.|url=https://www.mhi.com/news/story/20200507.html|access-date=20 July 2020|website=Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Ltd.|date=7 May 2020 |language=en}} MHI recorded a loss in FY 2020 partly because of the continuous delays of the first delivery of the SpaceJet.{{Cite news|date=6 February 2020|title=Mitsubishi postpones SpaceJet delivery again, books $4.5 billion special loss|language=en|work=Reuters|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-mitsubishi-spacejet-idUSKBN2000FI|access-date=22 July 2020}} At the height of the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] that crippled the aviation industry, MHI decided to put a halt to the project.{{Cite news |first1=Tim |last1=Kelly |first2=Maki |last2=Shiraki|date=23 October 2020|title=Japan's Mitsubishi Heavy to freeze development of SpaceJet regional jet: sources|language=en|work=Reuters|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-mhi-spacejet-development-idUSKBN2771W0|access-date=28 December 2020}} ===Defense=== In 2010, MHI commenced production of the [[Type 10]] advanced main battle tank, at a cost of $11.3 million per unit, to replace the [[Type 90 Kyū-maru|Type 90 tank]]. ===Energy=== {{See also|Mitsubishi FBR Systems|Atmea}} The nuclear business of MHI operates facilities in the cities of [[Kobe]] and [[Takasago, Hyōgo|Takasago]] in [[Hyōgo Prefecture|Hyogo]] Prefecture and in [[Yokohama, Kanagawa]] Prefecture. It also operates a nuclear fuel manufacturing plant in [[Tōkai, Ibaraki]] which processes 440 metric tons of Uranium per year. MHI has also developed the [[Mitsubishi APWR]] design. MHI has also signed a memorandum of understanding with [[Areva]] for the establishment of a joint venture, [[Atmea]], for their next reactor design ATMEA1.{{cite web|url=http://www.japancorp.net/Article.Asp?Art_ID=14804|title=JCN Newswire - Asia Press Release Distribution|access-date=7 February 2017|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130602085450/http://www.japancorp.net/Article.Asp?Art_ID=14804|archive-date=2 June 2013}} MHI has also been selected as the core company to develop a new generation of [[Fast Breeder Reactor]]s (FBR) by the Japanese government.{{cite web|url=http://www.uic.com.au/nip79.htm|title=Nuclear power in Japan|access-date=7 February 2017|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080303224931/http://www.uic.com.au/nip79.htm|archive-date=3 March 2008}} After that announcement was made, MHI established a new company, [[Mitsubishi FBR Systems]], Inc. (MFBR) specifically for the development and realization of FBR technology, starting what is likely to be the most aggressive corporate venture into FBR and [[Generation IV reactor]] technology.{{cite web|url=http://www.japancorp.net/Article.Asp?Art_ID=14745|title=JCN Newswire - Asia Press Release Distribution|access-date=7 February 2017|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130630205456/http://www.japancorp.net/Article.Asp?Art_ID=14745|archive-date=30 June 2013}} In 2011, Mitsubishi launched the Type-J gas turbines. These turbines were Mitsubishi's first combined-cycle gas turbines in the 1700°C-class, and also the first to surpass 60% operational efficiency. A key factor was the use of single-crystal turbine blades (MGA1700 alloy), which are considerably stronger than multi-crystal blades due to the lack of grain boundaries. In addition, the thermal barrier coating (TBC) of the blades have been improved, with the new thermally sprayed ceramic coating offering higher porosity and thus lower thermal conductivity than sintered materials. These upgrades allow for an inlet temperature of 1600 Celsius.{{Cite web |title=Development of Advanced Materials and Manufacturing Technologies for High-efficiency Gas Turbines |url=https://www.mhi.co.jp/technology/review/pdf/e524/e524005.pdf |website=www.mhi.co.jp}}{{Cite web |title=Test Results of the World's First 1,600oC J-series Gas Turbine |url=https://www.mhi-global.com/company/technology/review/pdf/e491/e491018.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151016100414/https://www.mhi-global.com/company/technology/review/pdf/e491/e491018.pdf |archive-date=16 October 2015 |website=www.mhi-global.com}}{{Cite web |title=Mitsubishi Power {{!}} M501J Series |url=https://power.mhi.com/products/gasturbines/lineup/m501j |access-date=28 April 2025 |website=Mitsubishi Power |language=en}} As of 2015, MHI was developing a $15.8 billion nuclear power plant in [[Sinop, Turkey]] in partnership with [[Itochu]] and [[Engie]], which would be its first overseas nuclear project.{{cite news|title=2 Japanese companies aim to fund 30% of Turkish nuclear project|url=http://asia.nikkei.com/Business/Deals/2-Japanese-companies-aim-to-fund-30-of-Turkish-nuclear-project|access-date=9 June 2015|work=[[Nikkei Asia]]|agency=Nikkei|date=8 June 2015}} The deal has been officially scrapped in January 2020, after the feasibility of the project was doubted.{{Cite web|title=Turkey / Contract For Sinop Nuclear Station 'Has Been Cancelled'|url=https://www.nucnet.org/news/contract-for-sinop-nuclear-station-has-been-cancelled-1-4-2020|access-date=22 July 2020|website=The Independent Global Nuclear News Agency|date=4 January 2019 }} MHI unsuccessfully attempted to acquire the energy business of [[Alstom]] in 2014 in order to develop its service network in Southeast Asia. MHI remains interested in acquisitions in the crude oil and gas sectors as of 2015.{{cite news|last1=Sekiguchi|first1=Keita|title=Mitsubishi Heavy opening up coffers for regional jet, acquisitions|url=http://asia.nikkei.com/Business/Companies/Mitsubishi-Heavy-opening-up-coffers-for-regional-jet-acquisitions|access-date=8 June 2015|work=[[Nikkei Asia]]|date=6 June 2015}} Following financial difficulties at [[Areva]], MHI announced in 2015 it would make a proposal to take a minority ownership stake in a new entity called inheriting Areva's nuclear reactor business and acquired a 19% stake in the entity in 2017. In 2018, the entity has been named [[Framatome]].{{cite news |url=http://www.world-nuclear-news.org/C-MHI-prepares-bid-for-stake-in-Arevas-reactor-business-0611154.html |title=MHI prepares bid for stake in Areva's reactor business |publisher=World Nuclear News |date=6 November 2015 |access-date=12 November 2015}}{{Cite web|title=MHI agrees to take 19.5% stake in New NP - World Nuclear News|url=https://world-nuclear-news.org/Articles/MHI-agrees-to-take-19-5-stake-in-New-NP|access-date=22 July 2020|website=world-nuclear-news.org |date=August 2017 }} In 2020, MHI eventually acquired Hitachi's [[gas turbine]] business unit after the two companies had merged their businesses to form a joint venture. Subsidiary Mitsubishi Power manufactures [[solid oxide fuel cell]]s (SOFCs) and hybrid SOFC and [[microturbine|micro gas turbine]] Megamie power generation systems.{{Cite web|title=Mitsubishi Power: SOFC|url=https://power.mhi.com/products/sofc}}{{Cite web |last=gasworld |date=2018-11-08 |title=MHPS selects 'MEGAMIE' as series name for its integrated fuel cell and gas turbine hybrid power generation system |url=https://www.gasworld.com/story/mhps-selects-megamie-as-series-name-for-its-integrated-fuel-cell-and-gas-turbine-hybrid-power-generation-system/2086358.article/ |access-date=2025-10-06 |website=gasworld |language=en-gb}} ===Shipbuilding=== Shipbuilding has been a core and historical founding activity for MHI. It was formally started in 1884 when Mitsubishi leased and then acquired the 'Nagasaki Shipyard & Machinery Works' company (founded in 1857 as 'Nagasaki Yotetsusho Foundry'{{cite web| url = http://www.msb.mhi.co.jp/en/company/history/index.html| title = Mitsubishi Shipbuilding Co., Ltd. {{!}} Company| access-date = 6 January 2019| archive-date = 7 January 2019| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190107015759/http://www.msb.mhi.co.jp/en/company/history/index.html| url-status = dead}}). Subsequently, Mitsubishi progressively became one of the major Japanese shipbuilding companies, building both commercial as well as military ships, including the [[Yamato-class battleship]], Musashi, of the [[Imperial Japanese Navy]] during [[World War II]]. MHI has [[shipbuilding]] facilities in [[Nagasaki, Nagasaki|Nagasaki]], [[Kobe]] and [[Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi|Shimonoseki]], Japan. {{Nihongo|''[[Nagasaki Shipyard & Machinery Works]]''|三菱重工長崎造船所 |Mitsubishi Juko Nagasaki Zosenjo}} is the primary shipbuilding division of MHI. [[Yonhap News Agency]] criticized Mitsubishi for rescuing Chinese victims while turning a blind eye to Korean victims.{{cite news |title=중국 노동자 피해보상 미쓰비시, 한국 피해자는 외면하나 |url=https://www.yna.co.kr/view/AKR20150724085300073 |agency=[[연합뉴스]] |date=24 July 2015 |access-date=6 March 2023}} On 28 November 2018, MHI was ordered by the [[South Korea Supreme Court]] to pay 150 million [[South Korean won|won]] ($133,000; £104,000) in compensation to 10 surviving Koreans who were victims of forced labor which the company oversaw during the [[Korea under Japanese rule|Japanese occupation of Korea]].{{cite news| url = https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/s-korea-court-orders-japans-mitsubishi-to-pay-compensation-for-wartime-forced-labor/2018/11/28/4f0a6616-f37e-11e8-9240-e8028a62c722_story.html| title = South Korea orders compsenation for forced labor during Japanese colonial rule - The Washington Post| newspaper = [[The Washington Post]]}}{{Cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-46381207|title=Mitsubishi Heavy ordered to compensate forced S Korean war workers|work=BBC News|date=29 November 2018}} Eighteen family members of other victims of the forced labour overseen by MHI, who had previously sued sometime before 2008, were now able to receive the compensation as well by the decision. All twenty-eight plaintiffs had previously filed a lawsuit in Japan, but had their lawsuit dismissed by the Supreme Court of Japan in 2008. The Japanese government has officially disputed the lawsuit and defined the verdict as "a breach of the international law", citing [[Treaty on Basic Relations between Japan and the Republic of Korea|the 1965 agreement]] which was made by the two nations to establish [[Diplomatic Relations|diplomatic relations]], since all of the "problems concerning property, rights, and interests" that had been existed between the two countries and respective peoples thereof during the occupation era "have been settled completely and finally".{{Cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/world-nation/story/2019-08-17/japan-korea-and-the-tquestion-of-how-to-pay-for-historic-wrongs|title=Japan, Korea and the messy question of how to pay for historic wrongs|date=17 August 2019|website=Los Angeles Times|language=en-US|access-date=9 September 2019}} During the [[2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine]], MHI did not withdraw from the Russian market. The [[Yale CELI List of Companies]], identifying how companies were reacting to Russia's invasion, identified MHI as one of the companies "defying demands for exit/reduction of activities".{{cite web|author= |title= Over 750 Companies Have Curtailed Operations in Russia—But Some Remain |website= [[Yale School of Management]] |url=https://som.yale.edu/story/2022/over-750-companies-have-curtailed-operations-russia-some-remain |access-date= 28 April 2022}} ==Notes== {{Reflist|30em}} ==References== {{Refbegin}} * {{citation | last1 = Chida | first1 = Momohei | authorlink2 = Peter Davies (economic historian) | first2 = Peter N. | last2 = Davies | date = 1990 | title = The Japanese Shipping and Shipbuilding Industries: A History of their Modern Growth | location = London | publisher = [[Athlone Press]] | isbn = 978-0-485-11271-9 | oclc = 20799046 }} * {{cite book |last=Fukasaku |first=Yukiko |date=1992 |title=Technology and Industrial Development in Pre–war Japan: Mitsubishi Nagasaki Shipyard 1884–1934 |location=London and New York|publisher=Routledge |isbn=0-415-06552-6}} * {{citation | last = Kizu | first = Shigetoshi | date = 1984 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=FJ2gPQAACAAJ&q=100+Year+History+of+the+Ships+of+Nippon+Yusen+Kaisha | title = A 100 Years' History of the Ships of Nippon Yusen Kaisha | location = Tokyo | publisher = NYK | isbn = 978-4-905551-20-1 | oclc = 16781302 }} * {{citation | authorlink = Richard Ponsonby-Fane | last = Ponsonby-Fane | first = Richard Arthur Brabazon | date = 1935 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=PdNAAAAAIAAJ&q=intitle:The+intitle:Nomeclature+intitle:of+intitle:the+intitle:NYK+intitle:Fleet | title = The Nomenclature of the N.Y.K. Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Ltd. (三菱重工業株式会社, Mitsubishi Jūkōgyō Kabushiki-kaisha; MHI) is a Japanese multinational engineering, electrical equipment and electronics corporation headquartered in Tokyo, Japan. MHI is one of the core companies of the Mitsubishi Group and its automobile division is the predecessor of Mitsubishi Motors.
MHI's products include aerospace and automotive components, air conditioners, elevators, forklift trucks, hydraulic equipment, printing machines, missiles, tanks, power systems, ships, aircraft, railway systems, and space launch vehicles. Through its defense-related activities, it is the world's 32nd-largest defense contractor measured by 2024 arms revenues and the largest based in Japan.
